overview: Across the lower Syr Darya, Aral shores and northern Caspian steppe, Oghuz clans made a political world that could move: herds, tents, chiefs and armed followings traveled while Yengi-kent anchored a winter court and caravan town. This was a loose, unequal confederation, not a modern nation or one uniform people. Its yabghu bargained with nobles and commanders, raised tribute, traded with oasis cities and joined alliances that shifted power across Inner Eurasia. The atlas’s 900 to 1000 date is only a display slice, and its polygon is wildly oversized, reaching from the Caspian almost to Lake Baikal. Read it as a locator for the western Oghuz Yabghu world, not verified control.

periods.title: A confederation beside river, desert and caravan road
periods.summary: Oghuz camps ranged around the Aral and Caspian while Yengi-kent connected a mobile court to lower-Syr settlements, Khwarazmian oases and long-distance exchange.

periods.title: An envoy meets the Oghuz
periods.summary: Ibn Fadlan crossed Oghuz country in 922. His vivid report preserves tents, hospitality, hierarchy and spoken words, but one foreign traveler’s route cannot describe everyone.

periods.title: A fortified crossroads grows
periods.summary: Dzhankent became densely built and fortified, mixing steppe, local and Khwarazmian material traditions. Archaeology supports a major exchange center without proving a monumental imperial capital.

periods.title: Alliances alter the western steppe
periods.summary: The yabghu allied with Sviatoslav against the Khazars in 965, and Oghuz forces joined Vladimir’s 985 campaign against Volga Bulgaria. Trade and raiding remained intertwined.

periods.title: Rival branches and new borderland choices
periods.summary: Seljuk-associated Oghuz moved toward Jand and the Muslim frontier, competing with Yengi-kent’s rulers. Merchant towns and military service opened paths that pasture politics alone could not.

periods.title: Conversion and division, not disappearance
periods.summary: The Seljuk family was Muslim by 992, but Islamization was gradual. Around the atlas endpoint, Oghuz elites and communities followed different political and religious routes.

periods.title: Beyond the map: two Oghuz futures
periods.summary: The older yabghu polity survived past 1000 while Seljuk leaders built a new imperial power farther south. Their rivalry ended one political form and amplified Oghuz influence.

items.text: The exact atlas record is approximate: one 900 to 1000 interval, one border file, and no earlier card. Those dates describe this imported display feature; they are not a founding certificate or an extinction date.

The decoded shape is one polygon with three rings and 595 positions. Its box runs from 50.3267°E to 116.9634°E, an implausible span from the Caspian region to far beyond the historically defensible Oghuz core.

Point tests put Yengi-kent, lower-Syr country, Ustyurt and Mangystau inside, but also enormous lands across Siberia and Mongolia. Bukhara, Samarkand, Merv, Gurganj, Kashgar, Balkh and the Khazar capital Itil test outside. The boundary is a drawing artifact, not a frontier survey.

“Oghuz” did not always name the same coalition. The relationship between western Oghuz on the Syr Darya and earlier Toquz Oghuz groupings in Mongolia remains disputed, so this card does not quietly merge them with the Uyghur Khaganate.

The project also has separate records for the later Seljuk Empire, an `oghuz` shape in 1100 to 1200, the Cuman-Kipchak confederation, Khwarazmian dynasty and modern Turkmenistan. They are historical neighbors or continuities, not spare pieces of this card.

The supreme ruler carried the title yabghu. Succession favored leading paternal lines, yet formal choice still mattered; rare popular assemblies and a noble council called the känkäsh meant rule depended on negotiation, not a button the yabghu could press.

An heir was an inal and an atabeg tutored him. A ruler’s wife held the title khatun and could matter at court; a sü-bashï commanded the army and might openly oppose the yabghu. That is elite education and court power, not evidence that all children attended school.

Officials collected tribute from mobile and settled communities, sometimes backed by mounted force. Society distinguished free full members from enslaved or dependent people, while hereditary begs and military households ranked above many pastoral families.

Warriors could make regional history, but “the Oghuz army” was not a permanent national force. Ibn Fadlan instead met commanders and leading households who consulted other elites and assembled armed followings.

A hard truth belongs beside the cavalry: enslavement was part of this world. Research at Dzhankent links the town to north to south traffic in livestock, furs and enslaved people; the evidence is serious, although one unusual enclosure remains an archaeological hypothesis.

Yengi-kent, “New Town,” identified with Dzhankent/Jankent, sat near the lower Syr Darya, cultivated oasis economies and routes running north and east. It let a mobile court winter near merchants, grain, craft goods and river-delta resources.

Archaeology complicates the capital story in a useful way. Dzhankent had older settlement beneath its Oghuz-era walls, dense tenth-century houses and several pottery traditions, but no proven palace or monumental “nomad capital” plan. Townspeople were culturally mixed.

Pastoralists exchanged skins, wool, pelts and livestock for grain and crafted goods. At Jand, Muslim merchant communities probably received products arriving from steppe and forest zones. The frontier was a marketplace as well as a battle line.

Cooking pots came in hand-built and wheel-thrown forms, and their recipes for clay and temper were not all the same. That variety points toward households, mobile traditions and southern workshops meeting in one town; the pottery classification is still unfinished.

Finds include glass, coins, a bronze vessel, querns and storage jars. None is a magic label saying “owned by an Oghuz family”: each object instead shows what could circulate through a fortified town shared by local, Khwarazmian, Turkic and Muslim-linked communities.

On the move, families used transportable haircloth tents and shifted camp with animals and pasture. Ibn Fadlan saw only part of Oghuz country in 922, so his roadside snapshot is precious without being everybody’s floor plan.

In town, a main room could have raised sufa platforms around the walls, one or two built-in tandirs, a central hearth and a pantry with jars sunk into the floor. Imagine a warm multipurpose room: cooking, sitting, sleeping, talking and work crowded together.

Fun hearth fact: some ceramic fireplace supports ended in paired ram heads. A family could heat dinner beside an object that was practical, decorative and perhaps meaningful, basically a very old kitchen gadget with horns.

Hospitality could create a cross-cultural safety net. Ibn Fadlan says a visiting merchant might form a reciprocal bond with an Oghuz host who supplied lodging and sheep; the visitor brought desired goods. Friendship here also did the work of travel insurance.

Textiles, caps, leather boots, silk, spices, nuts and grain appear in elite gift exchanges. They reveal taste and trade, but a diplomatic gift table is not an ordinary family wardrobe or shopping list. Some leaders were visibly richer than others.

Evidence for ordinary marriage, childcare and girls’ education is thin. Ibn Fadlan’s account notices elite households and a few sensational encounters, but later epics and modern customs cannot be pasted unchanged onto every tenth-century family.

sections.title: Herds, meals and one extremely tough cat

items.text: A 2026 isotope study of sixteen Dzhankent sheep found different birth seasons and feeding histories. Some animals grazed near the Syr Darya; others may have arrived from farther away. The city’s food system depended on many herders, not one synchronized super-flock.

Staggered lambing may have lengthened the seasons when milk and meat were available, and winter fodder may have included summer-cut plants or millet by-products. Those are careful scientific inferences, not a recovered weekly menu.

Sheep and goats dominate studied animal remains, with cattle, horses, camels, fish, birds and wild species also present. Bones show provisioning and work animals; they do not prove that each household ate every species or that meat was equally shared.

Querns, hearths, tandirs, cooking pots and large storage jars make daily labor visible: grinding, heating, baking, simmering, carrying and keeping supplies safe. Archaeology preserves the chores that victory lists forget.

Best resident: an adult tomcat dated about 775 to 940 survived broken bones, damaged teeth and other injuries while eating a rich protein diet and moving little. Researchers think sustained human care helped him live. We cannot name his owner, or prove he respected the pantry.

sections.title: Belief, learning and a voice on the page

items.text: In 922 many Oghuz people Ibn Fadlan met followed non-Islamic Turkic traditions. Islam spread unevenly through merchants, towns, alliances and leaders; the Seljuk family was Muslim by 992, while Yengi-kent’s ruling family appears to have converted around 1003.

Written-language sample: `بير تنكرى ,  bir täŋri ,  “one God.”` Ibn Fadlan heard Oghuz speech and wrote these words in Arabic script. This is an authentic tenth-century speech sample preserved by an outsider, not proof that Oghuz communities normally wrote Turkic this way.

Coins, Arabic graffiti, decorated lamps and a signet reading Muhammad show Islamic-linked writing in Dzhankent’s contact zone. An inscribed object could belong to a resident or arrive by trade, gift or war, so it cannot count every reader or believer.

Three eggs were discovered inside a pot with Arabic writing on their shells. The project reported that the words were still undeciphered. History occasionally hands archaeologists an inscribed egg and refuses to include the answer key.

There is no evidence here for universal schooling. Atabegs trained elite heirs; wider written culture came through towns and merchants. Kashgari’s great eleventh-century dictionary records Turkic life and Oghuz words, but its sole manuscript was copied in 1266: valuable later evidence, not a tenth-century schoolbook.

Ibn Fadlan says a sick person of means could be placed in a tent apart from the household while servants cared for him until recovery or death. That is evidence for social response and isolation, not proof of germ theory or a formal clinic.

His next detail is cruel: an enslaved or poor sick person might be abandoned. Care depended on status. The same passage that hints at practical isolation also exposes how sharply unequal survival could be.

No source in this research set securely documents an Oghuz physician, pharmacy, hospital or standard treatment. People surely tended wounds and illness, but naming herbs or cures without evidence would replace history with a costume drama.

One Dzhankent house had a tiled area draining dirty washwater into a buried jar or soakaway called a tashnau. That is real household sanitation, and specifically not a proven toilet, flush system or city sewer.

Ibn Fadlan complained that Oghuz people did not perform the post-toilet and ritual washings he expected, especially in winter. His religious standard and disgust shape the sentence. It cannot prove that everyone avoided washing, or that nobody had a latrine. Archaeology has not yet supplied a secure Oghuz-period toilet.

Late in the tenth century, attempts at regular taxation helped provoke revolt among mobile communities. Seljuk-associated leaders used that anger against Yengi-kent’s rulers. The crisis came from inside political relationships as well as outside enemies.

The Seljuk branch did not represent every Oghuz person. It moved south, adopted Islam, recruited followers and eventually won an empire. That astonishing sequel grew from Oghuz history, but later Seljuk palaces and art cannot be back-projected into a 922 steppe camp.

The older Yengi-kent polity survived past 1000. War with Seljuk rivals weakened it, and Kipchak pressure helped break it apart around the mid-eleventh century. The clean atlas endpoint is therefore a data handoff, not the night a civilization vanished.

Oghuz-speaking groups continued across Central Asia, Iran, the Caucasus and Anatolia. Modern Turkish, Azerbaijani and Turkmen belong to the Oghuz language branch. That is powerful linguistic continuity, not a claim that every modern speaker has one simple tenth-century ancestry.

What ended was one confederated center of power. Oghuz speech and identity continued through changing communities. The story is less a falling curtain than a road splitting into many roads, with no single modern population serving as a frozen copy of the year 1000.

ending.text: The year 1000 ends this atlas geometry, not the Oghuz. Yengi-kent’s yabghu polity continued into the eleventh century, then fractured through tax revolt, Seljuk rivalry and Kipchak pressure. Some Oghuz communities remained across the steppe; others moved south and west, and the Seljuk branch built a new empire. Oghuz languages and identities continued in changing forms. The ending is therefore political transformation and dispersal, with no single extinction year.
